Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Federal, state and municipal agencies staged an elaborate drill in the waters off New York City on Tuesday to prepare for the possibility of a nuclear or dirty-bomb attack from the water. A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passes a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday's terror drill. "We're a big city, and there are vulnerabilities," said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department. Agencies involved in Tuesday's test  emphasized they did not undertake it because of a specific threat against the city. However, Kelly said the city was taking no chances after a proclamation years ago by Osama bin Laden. "We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition," he said. In addition to increasing various agencies' preparedness for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly said Tuesday's well-publicized drill was meant to deter those who would perpetrate such an attack. "It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we're out there, that we have the capability to detect," Kelly said. Eight government agencies participated in the drill, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. The exercise took place at the entrance of New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge linking Staten Island to Brooklyn. Per the drill's plan, eight boats were to cross a checkpoint set up by authorities. They were on the lookout for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity -- a telltale sign of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more familiarly known as a dirty bomb. Some of the boats were decoys with no radioactive substances aboard, while others had actual radioactive isotopes planted in them. A radioactivity detector in the hull of the authorities' boats was to identify which vessels had radioactive substances in them. The devices are highly sensitive -- so much so that people who have recently had certain medical treatments can set them off. It was up to the authorities participating in the drill to sort the good boats from the bad -- and to intercept the bad. Only minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity within a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels then converged on the pleasure craft, while officials began to question the driver and his two passengers. Soon after, authorities boarded the boat and used a radiation detector, officially known as a radiological isotope identification detector, to produce a "spectrum" of the radiological material. They then transmitted the spectrum to the Department of Homeland Security's Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington to determine precisely what radiological material was aboard the boat. Within moments, the JAC radioed back with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that if used in large enough quantities could power a devastating dirty bomb. Sure enough, when a separate boat containing press and police officers sidled up to the apprehended craft soon afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors of officers onboard began to sound excitedly. NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said that, in part, the agencies chose to practice on leisure craft to illustrate that radiological weapons could be transported in deceptively benign-looking boats. "It doesn't require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat," Mogil said. James Waters, counterterrorism chief for the NYPD, said exercises like Tuesday's were vital because the stakes involved are so high. "Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic," he said. On an average day, not all incoming maritime traffic in New York City is subjected to the radioactivity tests performed at Tuesday's drill. An NYPD official declined to specify what percentage of boats normally undergo such screening.

**NEW YORK** — In a major effort to bolster maritime security and defend against potential high-yield terror threats, federal, state, and local law enforcement authorities recently executed a comprehensive, multi-vessel tactical exercise in the waters of New York Harbor. Designed to counter the threat of a seaborne nuclear weapon or radiological "dirty bomb," the operation brought together eight separate government agencies to test advanced detection technologies, refine joint response protocols, and send a clear signal of deterrence to potential adversaries.

### A Critical Maritime Gateway

New York Harbor is one of the world’s busiest and most economically vital maritime transit hubs, accommodating thousands of commercial cargo ships, ferry routes, fishing vessels, and private pleasure craft every day. However, this high volume of maritime traffic also presents a complex security challenge. The sheer density of open water and narrow channels offers potential cover for illicit operations, including the smuggling of dangerous non-conventional weapons. 

To address this strategic vulnerability, the coordinated exercise simulated a high-stakes threat scenario: an attempt by a hostile group to sneak a radiological dispersal device (RDD)—commonly known as a dirty bomb—or an improvised nuclear device (IND) into the metropolitan area via watercraft.

### Advanced Detection in Action

The cornerstone of the operation was the deployed technology. Participating agencies—including the U.S. Coast Guard, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the New York City Police Department (NYPD) Maritime Bureau, the Port Authority Police Department, the New York State Police, the Department of Energy’s National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), and local emergency management services—deployed a fleet of specialized patrol boats equipped with state-of-the-art radiation detection systems.

During the drill, tactical vessels established mobile security checkpoints and active sweep zones along critical maritime choke points, including the Verrazzano-Narrows, the Kill Van Kull, and the approaches to the Hudson and East Rivers. Participating vessels were outfitted with high-sensitivity gamma and neutron sensors, capable of scanning nearby watercraft from a distance without disrupting normal transit traffic. Specialized boarding teams were also equipped with portable, backpack-mounted radiation detectors and handheld radioisotope identification devices (RIIDs).

To rigorously test the system, "red team" decoy boats carrying small, safe, and tightly controlled calibration isotopes were blended into the general flow of harbor traffic. Sensor arrays mounted on the search vessels successfully picked up the signatures, automatically alerted operators, and correctly identified the specific radioactive isotopes embedded in the target craft within seconds.

### Strengthening Inter-Agency Interoperability

Beyond validating physical technology, the exercise served as a rigorous stress test for the command-and-control framework that links these diverse agencies. Historically, cross-agency communication and data sharing have posed operational hurdles during complex, fast-moving crises.

During the harbor exercise, search data and sensor telemetry were streamed in real time to a centralized Joint Operations Center. This unified command structure ensured that if a high-value radiological match was detected, tactical assets—including armed interdiction craft and specialized bomb disposal units—could be immediately vector-routed to intercept, isolate, and secure the target vessel. 

Official evaluations of the exercise confirmed that all simulated radiological targets were successfully detected, tracked, and intercepted, demonstrating a high level of operational readiness and cross-agency synchronization.

### Strategic Deterrence and Future Preparedness

While the primary objective of the drill was operational readiness, officials stressed that its high visibility was entirely intentional. By conducting such an elaborate and multi-faceted operation in broad daylight within sight of the Manhattan skyline, authorities aimed to project an unmistakable image of readiness.

As maritime threats continue to evolve in complexity, officials confirmed that the lessons learned from this exercise will be integrated into future tactical training programs. Regular joint drills of this scale will remain a cornerstone of the nation’s strategy to safeguard its vital ports, coastal communities, and critical national infrastructure against radiological threats.

**NYPD and Coast Guard launch high-stakes maritime drill to stop potential 'dirty bomb' threat in NY Harbor**

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Swarming the waters beneath the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and fanning out near the Statue of Liberty, law enforcement tactical boats and low-flying helicopters staged a massive joint security exercise Thursday, simulating a nightmare scenario: an intercepted cargo vessel carrying a smuggled "dirty bomb" heading toward New York City.

The high-intensity exercise, coordinated by the NYPD’s Counterterrorism Bureau and the U.S. Coast Guard, was designed to test the region’s capability to detect, track, and neutralize a radiological threat before it can reach the nation's most densely populated metropolis. 

For hours, the normally routine maritime traffic of New York Harbor was punctuated by the roar of NYPD Bell 429 helicopters hovering overhead and high-speed Coast Guard response craft cutting through the choppy waters. 

"New York City remains the premier target for terrorists around the globe, and our waterways are the city's front door," a senior NYPD counterterrorism official told CNN on the scene. "If a threat is coming by sea, we cannot afford to wait until it hits the dock. We have to interdict it out here."

### High-tech hunting on the water

The core of Thursday's exercise focused on detecting a Radiological Dispersal Device (RDD)—commonly known as a "dirty bomb"—which uses conventional explosives to scatter radioactive material over a targeted area. While less destructive than a nuclear warhead, an RDD detonation in Manhattan could cause widespread panic, massive economic disruption, and long-term environmental contamination.

During the scenario, a "rogue" container ship acting as a decoy vessel was injected with a safe, low-level radioactive isotope to test the agencies' detection capabilities. 

Equipped with specialized radiation sensors—ranging from wearable belt detectors on tactical officers to heavy-duty maritime detection arrays mounted on NYPD Harbor Unit vessels—officers scanned the harbor to pinpoint the target. 

Once the "dirty bomb" signature was confirmed, heavily armed boarding teams from the Coast Guard’s Maritime Safety and Security Team (MSST) and the NYPD’s Emergency Service Unit (ESU) executed a tactical breach of the vessel. Fast-roping from helicopters onto the ship's deck, the joint teams simulated neutralizing non-compliant crew members and securing the hazardous payload.

### A complex, evolving threat

New York Harbor spans over 300 square miles of complex waterways, bordered by thousands of miles of shoreline, making it one of the most challenging environments in the country to secure. Millions of tons of cargo pass through the Port of New York and New Jersey every year.

Security experts emphasize that inter-agency communication is often the biggest hurdle during a real-world crisis. Thursday's drill was specifically engineered to test real-time intelligence sharing between the federal government and local police.

"Exercises like this ensure that when a real threat emerges, the first time the Coast Guard and the NYPD are talking to each other isn't during the crisis," Coast Guard Captain of the Port Zeita Merchant said in a statement following the exercise. "Our seamless integration is what keeps this port, and this city, safe."

Federal officials have long worried about the proliferation of radiological materials globally, which could potentially be acquired on the black market and smuggled into major Western ports. While intelligence officials maintain there is currently "no specific, credible threat" involving a dirty bomb in New York, Thursday's drill underscores the intense preparation happening behind the scenes.

"We train for the worst-case scenario every single day," the NYPD official said as the tactical craft returned to base. "So that the worst-case scenario never happens."

**NEW YORK** — Against the backdrop of the soaring spans of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, a fleet of tactical patrol boats, federal cutters, and low-flying helicopters descended on the waters of New York Harbor on Thursday in one of the largest maritime counter-terrorism exercises in the region's history. 

The multi-agency drill, coordinated by the NYPD Counterterrorism Bureau alongside the U.S. Coast Guard, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and regional law enforcement partners, was designed to test the city’s defense against a nightmare scenario: a illicit radiological weapon smuggled into the nation’s largest metropolis via boat.

For several hours, the narrow strait connecting Upper and Lower New York Bays was transformed into a high-tech security checkpoint. The primary objective was to evaluate advanced mobile radiation detection equipment capable of scanning moving vessels, specifically targeting recreational "pleasure craft" that weave through the harbor’s heavy commercial traffic every day.

### Detecting the Invisible: The Caesium-137 Test

During the drill, covert "decoy" pleasure craft were deployed into the waters among unsuspecting local maritime traffic. Hidden aboard these test boats were sealed, controlled sources of dangerous radioactive isotopes—specifically **Caesium-137**, a gamma-emitting industrial isotope frequently cited by security experts as a primary component for a potential "dirty bomb" or Radiological Dispersal Device (RDD).

Law enforcement vessels equipped with specialized maritime radiation sensors, along with tactical operators carrying handheld spectroscopic meters, swept the harbor. The technology was tasked with not only detecting trace radiological signatures from dozens of yards away, but also instantly analyzing the energy spectrum to distinguish between harmless background radiation—such as benign medical isotopes used by recent cancer patients—and dangerous threat materials like Caesium-137 or enriched uranium.

"New York Harbor is the front door to our city, and we cannot afford a single blind spot," said NYPD Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly, addressing reporters at a tactical briefing site overlooking the bridge in Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island. "A weaponized radiological device brought through these waterways could cause catastrophic economic and physical damage. The capability to detect nuclear and radiological materials like Caesium-137 at sea, before a vessel gets anywhere near our bridges or population centers, is an essential line of defense."

Once a decoy boat emitting the synthetic threat signature was flagged by the automated sensors, armed NYPD Harbor Unit crews and Coast Guard Maritime Safety and Security Teams (MSST) executed rapid-interception maneuvers, rushing the target vessel, establishing a perimeter, and deploying boarding teams in full protective gear to neutralize the mock threat.

### Unprecedented Interagency Coordination

The exercise brought together over 300 personnel, dozens of watercraft, and aerial surveillance assets equipped with down-link video technology that streamed real-time radiological mapping data back to the NYPD’s Lower Manhattan Security Initiative command center.

Federal officials emphasized that maritime environments present unique technical challenges for radiation detection, including wave interference, background radiation from seawater, and the rapid movement of targets.

"Searching for a hidden radiological source on a moving pleasure craft in open water is the technological equivalent of finding a needle in a moving haystack," said a senior DHS Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (CWMD) official involved in the operation. "This drill proved that our sensor networks can isolate a specific isotope like Caesium-137 in real time, giving operational commanders the exact data they need to interdict a threat before it reaches a critical infrastructure point like the Verrazzano Bridge."

### The Rationale Behind a Public Drill

Unlike many covert security operations, city and federal officials took deliberate steps to publicize Thursday’s exercise in advance, notifying the public, local mariners, and news outlets. Officials cited a three-fold rationale for the openness: managing public safety, fostering community vigilance, and projecting a clear strategic deterrent.

Commissioner Kelly addressed the decision to make the high-visibility drill so public, framing it as a crucial element of the department's broader counter-terrorism strategy.

"First, transparency prevents panic. When people see tactical gunboats and tactical teams operating under the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, we want them to know their city is being defended, not under attack," Kelly explained. 

"Second, and just as importantly, publicizing these exercises serves as a direct message of deterrence to anyone who might wish to do this city harm," Kelly added. "We want our adversaries to see the level of sophistication, the seamless agency coordination, and the technology waiting for them. New York is a hard target, on land and on the water."

Officials also noted that publicizing the exercise serves to remind the local boating community—often referred to as the "eyes and ears" of the harbor—to report unusual behavior to the NYPD's Operation Sentinel or the Coast Guard's National Response Center.

By late afternoon, as the exercise concluded and tactical units stood down, officials reported that all simulated radiological targets, including all hidden Caesium-137 sources, were successfully identified and intercepted within target timeframes. Security agencies plan to analyze the telemetry data collected during the drill to further refine detection algorithms for future harbor surveillance.

**NEW YORK** — Gunfire echoed off the hull of a commercial tugboat in Upper New York Bay on Tuesday morning as tactical teams in fast-response craft converged on the vessel, swarming its deck under the cover of low-flying helicopters. 

The high-intensity scene was not a real-world crisis, but the climax of "Operation Trident Shield"—a massive, joint counter-terrorism exercise designed to test how federal, state, and local agencies would stop a "dirty bomb" from entering New York City by water.

Organized by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in coordination with the NYPD, the U.S. Coast Guard, the FBI, and the Port Authority Police, the daylong drill simulated a complex, high-stakes threat: a hostile group attempting to transport a Radiological Dispersal Device (RDD) hidden aboard a ship into Lower Manhattan.

A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to scatter radioactive material. While it lacks the devastating blast yield of a nuclear weapon, an RDD detonated in a densely populated hub like New York Harbor could cause widespread panic, economic paralysis, and long-term environmental contamination.

"New York City remains the nation's premier target, and our waterways represent both a vital economic artery and a vulnerable vector," said NYPD First Deputy Commissioner Edward Caban during a afternoon briefing at Battery Park. "Today was about ensuring that if a threat approaches from the water, the handoff between federal intelligence, maritime law enforcement, and local tactical units is seamless and instant."

The exercise began in the early morning hours off the coast of New Jersey, where simulated intelligence flagged a suspicious vessel bound for the East River. Coast Guard cutters equipped with long-range radiological detection sensors intercepted the boat’s signal, triggering an immediate, multi-agency response.

Within minutes, a unified command center established a temporary security zone around the harbor. Coast Guard Maritime Safety and Security Teams (MSST) worked alongside NYPD Harbor Unit vessels to isolate the target ship. Meanwhile, FBI SWAT operators and NYPD Emergency Service Unit (ESU) officers conducted a dynamic boarding operation to neutralize the mock hostiles and secure the vessel.

Once the ship was seized, specialized hazmat and bomb squad technicians from the FDNY and the DHS Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (CWMD) Office boarded to disarm the simulated device and contain the radioactive source.

"Exercises like Trident Shield push our capabilities to the limit in a controlled environment so that we are flawless in an uncontrolled one," said Capt. Zeita Merchant, Commander of Coast Guard Sector New York. "The maritime domain is vast and dynamic. No single agency can secure it alone."

New York City features more than 520 miles of coastline, busy commercial shipping lanes, and thousands of recreational boats operating daily. Securing such a vast area against asymmetric threats requires constant vigilance and advanced technology, including radiation-detection devices mounted on police boats, helicopters, and even individual officers' vests.

Officials noted that while there is currently no specific, credible radiological threat to New York City, exercises of this scale are conducted periodically to refine tactical communication, test cutting-edge detection gear, and ensure that overlapping jurisdictional lines do not slow down a response.

By late Tuesday afternoon, the exercise concluded, and normal maritime traffic resumed in the harbor. 

"The message from today is simple," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge Michael Driscoll. "If a threat comes by land, air, or sea, we are watching, we are ready, and we will stop it before it reaches our shores."

**NYC tests nuclear response protocols in massive 6-hour multi-agency exercise featuring 'dirty bomb' decoys**

**By** Ryan Young and Sarah Jorgensen, CNN
**Updated** 8:14 AM EDT, Tuesday, October 24, 2023

**(CNN) —** In one of the most complex counter-terrorism exercises staged in the United States this year, federal, state, and local agencies converged on Manhattan overnight to execute a high-stakes, six-hour simulation of a nuclear threat targeting New York City.

The covert drill, code-named "Operation Gotham Sentinel," unfolded between 10:00 p.m. Monday and 4:00 a.m. Tuesday. It was designed to stress-test the city’s defense grid against a simulated radiological attack, featuring rogue vehicles, decoy targets, and actual, low-level radioactive isotopes safely monitored by federal scientists.

According to officials familiar with the exercise, the scenario centered on an extremist cell attempting to transport a "dirty bomb"—a conventional explosive packed with radioactive material—into the heart of Midtown Manhattan.

To make the exercise as realistic as possible, organizers deployed three unmarked delivery vans throughout the city. Two acted as decoys, while one carried trace, non-hazardous amounts of medical-grade radioactive isotopes—specifically Cobalt-60 and Cesium-137—to trigger real-time alerts on local and federal detection networks.

"You cannot effectively test a radiation detection grid with computer simulations alone," said a senior official with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the operation. "We needed to know if our sensors, scattered across bridges, tunnels, and patrol units, could distinguish the true threat from background noise and tactical decoys in a dense urban environment."

### Eight agencies, one response grid

The six-hour operation required seamless real-time coordination among eight separate government entities:

1. **Department of Homeland Security (DHS):** Overseas threat tracking and federal resource mobilization.
2. **New York City Police Department (NYPD):** Tactical response, perimeter control, and ground surveillance.
3. **Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY):** Hazmat operations and mock mass-decontamination protocols.
4. **Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI):** Leading the Joint Terrorism Task Force (JTTF) command center.
5. **U.S. Department of Energy (DOE / NNSA):** Deploying the Nuclear Emergency Support Team (NEST) to identify and render safe radiological material.
6. **Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA):** Coordinating regional disaster response capabilities.
7. **Port Authority Police Department (PAPD):** Monitoring transit hubs, bridges, and tunnels.
8. **New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services (DHSES):** Integrating state-level intelligence and logistics.

### How the six-hour drill unfolded

The exercise commenced at 10:00 p.m. when a Port Authority sensor at the Lincoln Tunnel registered a preliminary radiological hit from a commercial van entering Manhattan. Within minutes, the NYPD Counterterrorism Bureau and the FBI JTTF established a joint tactical command center at an undisclosed location in Lower Manhattan.

By midnight, the drill took a complex turn. The suspect vehicle split off, and two decoy vans carrying industrial materials designed to mask radiation signatures entered the grid via the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel.

Low-flying DOE helicopters equipped with aerial radiation detection equipment swept across the Manhattan skyline, tracking the heat and radiological signatures while NYPD ground units systematically intercepted the decoy vehicles near Times Square and the Financial District. 

The primary target—the vehicle containing the active test isotopes—was ultimately pinned down by NYPD Emergency Service Unit (ESU) officers and FBI SWAT at 2:30 a.m. inside a staging area at the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

"The decoy strategy was meant to throw off our response protocols and force inter-agency communications to break down," NYPD Chief of Counterterrorism James Waters told reporters early Tuesday morning following the conclusion of the exercise. "It forced us to rely heavily on DHS data-sharing and DOE radiological experts to confirm where the real threat was located before moving in."

During the final two hours of the simulation, FDNY Hazmat crews and DOE NEST teams performed a mock "render-safe" procedure, isolating the radioactive payload using specialized lead containment transport vehicles, while establishing a mock decontamination corridor for exposed officers.

### Public impact minimized

Authorities kept public disruption to a minimum by conducting the bulk of the exercise in industrial areas and utilizing temporary, rolling closures on major thoroughfares. Sleeping New Yorkers were largely unaware of the high-octane exercise playing out on their streets, though brief sightings of heavily armed tactical teams and specialized Hazmat units prompted a flurry of posts on social media overnight.

Officials emphasized that "Operation Gotham Sentinel" was a long-planned, routine readiness exercise and was not conducted in response to any specific or credible threat against New York City.

However, DHS officials acknowledged that the geopolitical climate has prompted federal agencies to re-evaluate response times for weapons of mass destruction (WMD) scenarios in major American metropolitan areas.

"The tactics used by adversary groups evolve constantly," the DHS official said. "Last night proved that while the technology to track these threats is advanced, the human element—the ability of eight different agencies to speak the same language under extreme time pressure—is what ultimately saves lives."

**New York City Harbor Tests Defenses Against Radiological Threats in Major Exercise**

**NEW YORK (CNN) --** Against the iconic backdrop of the Manhattan skyline, federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies launched a multi-agency counter-terrorism exercise in the waters surrounding New York City on Tuesday, simulating a high-stakes scenario: stopping a smuggled radiological device before it reaches the shore.

The drill, coordinated by the U.S. Coast Guard alongside the NYPD, the FBI, and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), turned the busy waterways of New York Harbor into a proving ground for the nation's most advanced maritime defense capabilities. 

"The maritime environment presents unique challenges," said NYPD Deputy Commissioner of Counterterrorism Thomas Galati during a press briefing at Fort Wadsworth in Staten Island. "With thousands of commercial ships, ferries, and recreational boats traversing these waters daily, our goal is to find the needle in a haystack before that haystack reaches a crowded pier."

### A Layered Defense Against 'Dirty Bombs'

The primary focus of Tuesday's operation was testing the city’s defense against a potential "dirty bomb"—a conventional explosive packed with radioactive material—or a smuggled nuclear component.

Officials outlined a multi-layered detection strategy that begins miles before a suspicious vessel ever enters Upper New York Bay.

According to Coast Guard officials, incoming commercial vessel traffic is first screened electronically using the Automated Identification System (AIS) and intelligence databases managed by the National Targeting Center. Vessels deemed "high risk" based on their origin, crew manifest, or erratic travel patterns are flagged for offshore interception.

As boats approach the harbor, the physical inspection begins. Tactical teams deployed aboard high-speed response craft are equipped with specialized detection gear designed to scan passing traffic without disrupting the flow of commerce:

* **Boat-Mounted Radiation Monitors:** NYPD Harbor Craft and Coast Guard cutters are outfitted with highly sensitive gamma and neutron detectors. These sensors can pick up minute signatures of radiation emitted from nearby vessels, even through steel hulls.
* **Personal Radiation Detectors (PRDs):** Every boarding officer wears a compact PRD on their tactical vest. These wearable devices act as a continuous baseline monitor, alerting the officer silently via vibration if radiation levels spike.
* **Radionuclide Identification Devices (RIIDs):** If a radiation source is detected, boarding teams deploy hand-held RIIDs. These sophisticated devices analyze the specific energy spectrum of the radiation to determine its exact isotope within seconds. 

"One of our biggest operational hurdles is sorting out 'false positives,'" explained a DHS official participating in the exercise. "Cat litter, ceramic tiles, bananas, and even individuals who recently underwent medical procedures like thyroid treatment emit natural or harmless radiation. The technology allows us to instantly differentiate between iodine-131 used in a hospital and cesium-137 or enriched uranium intended for a weapon."

### Boarding and Interdiction

During Tuesday’s simulated exercise, a rogue commercial vessel played the role of a hostile threat. 

Cruising near the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the target ship triggered a simulated alarm on a patrolling NYPD vessel. Within minutes, a joint boarding team—comprising NYPD Tactical Units and Coast Guard Maritime Safety and Security Teams (MSST)—executed a tactical vectoring maneuver.

Under the cover of a hovering NYPD helicopter, fast-response boats surrounded the target vessel. Armed boarding teams ascended the ship’s sides using hook-and-climb ladders, securing the bridge and engine room while specialized chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) specialists swept the cargo hold.

Once the simulated radiological threat was identified, a specialized FBI Hazardous Devices Team was called in via boat to render the device safe, while the vessel was escorted to a secure, isolated mooring zone away from population centers.

### Constant Vigilance in the Post-9/11 Era

New York Harbor is one of the busiest port complexes in the United States, generating billions of dollars in economic activity. Officials emphasized that exercises like Tuesday's are not conducted in response to a specific, actionable threat, but are part of a routine effort to refine inter-agency communication and keep technology updated.

"The threat landscape is constantly evolving," said Coast Guard Captain of the Port Zeita Merchant. "An exercise like this ensures that when a real-world threat emerges, there is zero hesitation. The seamless integration of federal intelligence and local tactical boots on the water is what keeps this harbor secure."

Officials stated that similar unannounced sweeps and visible multi-agency patrols will continue throughout the week across the Hudson River, East River, and Kill Van Kull waterways.
